title: Bengal police visit homes of voters appealing roll deletions; Opposition cries foul
dek: Police in at least eight districts have collected documents from people whose appeals are pending before SIR tribunals. The state electoral office says it was not told; the BJP defends the checks on security grounds.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
Police in several West Bengal districts have been going to the homes of voters whose names were struck off the electoral rolls and who have appealed to the special intensive revision (SIR) tribunals, asking for identity papers, birth and school certificates and land records, according to reports. Opposition parties say the drive is unlawful and amounts to running a "police state"; the BJP, which governs the state, says it is about law and order and internal security.

The office of the state's Chief Electoral Officer said it was unaware that police were collecting the data, according to reports. An additional chief electoral officer denied that any instruction had been sent to the police, while a senior officer described it as a local "drive", according to reports. No written order authorising the visits has been made public.

## What is happening

Reports name Malda, Jalpaiguri, South Dinajpur, Uttar Dinajpur, Murshidabad, Purba Medinipur, East Burdwan, Bankura, South 24 Parganas, Howrah and Hooghly among the districts where police have visited homes or held camps since Tuesday. In Howrah, a verification camp was reported at a school, and visits were reported in areas under the Jagacha, Chatterjeehat and Golabari police stations.

The forms used asked for the voter's identity card number, Assembly constituency and police station, birth and school certificates, land documents, the parents' educational qualifications, and whether the voter's and the parents' names appeared on the 2002 electoral roll, according to reports. In Goghat in Hooghly, residents objected when police could not explain the purpose of the visits, and some officers left, according to reports.

Some officials said the aim was to check eligibility for state welfare schemes; others linked it to speeding up the tribunals' scrutiny of appeals, according to reports. Police officials in some districts acknowledged carrying out the checks.

## What each side says

Jawhar Sircar, a retired civil servant and former Rajya Sabha member, said it was "scary and illegal for the state government to send police to the voter's homes" to collect details of those who have appealed to the tribunals, in a social media post, according to reports. He called it a "knee-jerk reaction" to the Supreme Court's direction to fast-track the appeals.

Mohammed Salim, the CPI(M)'s state secretary, urged voters to ask officers under whose authority they were acting and not to hand over original documents, according to reports. The Association for Protection of Civil Rights (APCR) in West Bengal said the job belonged to booth-level officers and electoral registration officers, who answer to the Election Commission, and demanded that any order be made public. The SUCI(C) held protest rallies in several districts on Thursday.

The BJP defended the exercise, citing law and order and internal security, according to reports.

## Background

About 90 lakh names were removed from West Bengal's rolls in this year's SIR, more than 60 lakh of them as dead, shifted, absent or duplicate entries, according to reports citing Election Commission data. People whose names were removed can appeal to tribunals set up on the Supreme Court's directions and staffed by former High Court judges, according to reports.

A citizens' group, the Votadhikar Suraksha Samanway Samity, said more than 22 lakh deleted voters who had appealed had not yet received relief, and questioned about 16 lakh appeals it said had been filed on the Election Commission's side against voters whom judicial officers had found eligible. It submitted a memorandum to the additional chief electoral officer asking for the SIR to be scrapped, welfare benefits restored and all appeals settled before any election in the state. Opposition parties and petitioners say disputed deletions exceeded the winning margins in dozens of seats in this year's Assembly election.

## What happens next

The APCR said it would write to the authorities seeking the basis for the visits. Neither the state government nor the state police has issued a public statement on who ordered the checks. The tribunals continue to hear appeals under the Supreme Court's direction to decide them quickly.
